newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian government suffers pre-election setback.
newsitem.headline: Canadian government suffers pre-election setback.

text.p: A Canadian judge on Thursday rejected the Liberal federal government's attempts to cut off an inquiry into Canadian peacekeeping in Somalia, handing it a setback just as it was preparing for general elections.

The 2-year-old Somalia Inquiry had turned into an embarrassment for Prime Minister Jean Chretien's government, which had ordered it to stop taking testimony by the end of March and write a report by the end of June.
Analysts had almost universally interpreted this as a move to get the inquiry off the news in case Chretien called federal elections for June 2 or June 9, as is widely expected.

Federal Court Justice Sandra Simpson, in a decision rendered in Vancouver, set aside the government's order to stop the inquiry. She said this had "the practical effect of putting the Commission of Inquiry in a position to continue its hearings and the preparation of its report on its full mandate without deadlines until the (government) chooses to take further action."
Simpson said the government could either formally lift the deadline completely or curtail the inquiry's mandate and force it formally to ignore certain events or matters.

The government can appeal the decision and hope to tie it up in the courts until after the elections, but it could become a campaign issue if it openly truncated the mandate of a sorry episode of Canadian peacekeeping.
Defense Minister Doug Young declared that the government was not prepared to extend the deadline for wrapping up the commission: "The commission has already had three extensions."
He said it was too early to decide whether or not to appeal, but said the government would be assessing the options set out by Simpson "to ensure the commission meets its reporting date."

On March 4, 1993, Canadian peacekeepers shot two Somalis in the back as they fled, and on March 16 they tortured to death Somali teen-ager Shidane Arone. The inquiry has been able to cover the events of March 4, and charges that officials in Ottawa illegally altered public documents much later, but not the events of March 16 or general charges of a cover-up.
A court challenge was brought by John Dixon, an aide to former Defense Minister Kim Campbell, who wanted a chance to tell his side of the story.

"The message from the court to the government is if you want this commission not to investigate the cover-up of Shidane Arone, then you must speak in clear and unmistakable language and take the political responsibility for your actions," Dixon's lawyer Joseph Arvay said in Vancouver.

Chretien was elected in October 1993 and is not required to call new elections until October 1998. But preparations for a campaign have been well under way and the prime minister's schedule was being cleared for a possible June election.
The other possible time that has been broached is in October but Chretien has a heavy schedule of international engagements in the fall that could preoccupy him.
